Not affiliated with or endorsed by the Sarbanes Oxley Compliance Professionals Association (SOXCPA), the SEC or the PCAOB. Checked 31 Oct 2026.
overview: This domain covers Titles I and II of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. Title I created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB), a nonprofit body under SEC oversight that registers, sets standards for, inspects and disciplines the audit firms of public companies. Title II protects auditor independence: it bans certain non-audit services, puts the audit committee in charge of approving the rest, rotates audit partners, requires the auditor to report key matters to the audit committee, and imposes a cooling-off period before audit staff join a client in a top finance role.
analogy: Think of a professional sports league. Referees (audit firms) judge whether teams (public companies) follow the rules. A referees' association (the PCAOB) licenses the referees, writes their rulebook, reviews game footage and suspends bad referees, while the league commissioner (the SEC) must sign off on its rules and can overturn its suspensions. To stay neutral, a referee may not also coach a team they judge (prohibited services), senior referees swap teams after five seasons (partner rotation), and a referee cannot officiate a team right after joining its coaching staff (the cooling-off period).

parts.name: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board

topics.overview: Section 101 creates the PCAOB as a nonprofit corporation, not a government agency, with five full-time members. Section 109 funds it through accounting support fees paid mainly by issuers (and, since 2010, brokers and dealers), and Section 107 places it under SEC oversight: the SEC approves its rules and budget and reviews its sanctions.
can_do: Describe the PCAOB's legal status and tell it apart from the SEC
State the Board's size, the two-CPA limit and how members are appointed
Explain who pays the accounting support fee and on what basis
Name the SEC's powers over Board rules, sanctions and members

subtopics.name: The PCAOB's Legal Status and Duties
subtopics.definition: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) is a nonprofit corporation, not a government agency, created by Section 101 to oversee audits of companies under the securities laws.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam items often call the PCAOB a government agency or an SEC division. Its status explains why the SEC oversees it and why its staff are not federal employees.
how_it_works: Section 101(a) creates the Board as a nonprofit corporation that lasts until Congress dissolves it.
Section 101(b) says it is not a U.S. government agency, and its members and staff are not federal officers or employees.
Section 101(c) lists its duties: register firms, set standards, inspect, investigate and discipline, and enforce compliance.
Dodd-Frank extended its oversight from audits of issuers to audits of brokers and dealers (15 U.S.C. 7211, as amended in 2010).
It files an annual report, with audited financial statements, with the SEC (Section 101(h)).
subtopics.example: At an onboarding session for a bank's new compliance staff, Marta, the compliance lead, draws three boxes: the SEC, the PCAOB and the bank's audit firm. A trainee links the PCAOB box directly to the bank. Marta redraws the lines from the PCAOB to the audit firm and from the SEC to both the PCAOB and the bank, then adds the chart to the team's SOX reference pack.

review: Compare training materials' description of the PCAOB with Section 101
Trace each oversight line in the compliance chart to a statute
evidence: Section 101 text from the official public law
Training deck and reference chart showing PCAOB and SEC roles
audit_focus.recommend: Have the compliance team correct any material that calls the PCAOB a government agency or an issuer regulator.
audit_focus.decides: Congress set the Board's status; the SEC oversees the Board

subtopics.isaca_rule: The PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation, not a federal agency. It oversees registered audit firms and their associated persons; the SEC oversees both the issuers and the PCAOB.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB is part of the SEC, so its staff are federal employees.
exam_traps.why: Section 101(b) says the Board is not a government agency and its members and staff are not federal officers or employees. The SEC oversees it from outside.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB regulates public companies directly.
exam_traps.why: The Board registers, inspects and disciplines audit firms and their associated persons. Issuers answer to the SEC.

key_terms.definition: An audit firm registered with the PCAOB under Section 102, the only kind allowed to audit issuers.
A partner, accountant, employee or contractor who shares in a firm's profits or acts for it on audit reports (Section 2(a)(9)).

subtopics.name: Board Membership and Terms
subtopics.definition: The PCAOB has five full-time members appointed by the SEC, of whom two, and only two, are or have been certified public accountants (CPAs).
subtopics.why_it_matters: Capping CPA seats keeps the profession from controlling its own regulator, and full-time service keeps members free of ties to audit firms.
how_it_works: Five members serve full time and may hold no other job or business activity while on the Board (Section 101(e)(1) and (3)).
Two and only two members are or have been CPAs; a CPA chair must not have practiced for at least five years before appointment (Section 101(e)(2)).
The SEC appoints members after consulting the Federal Reserve chair and the Treasury Secretary (Section 101(e)(4)).
Terms are five years and staggered, and no one may serve more than two terms (Section 101(e)(5)).
Members may not share in an audit firm's profits, apart from fixed retirement payments (Section 101(e)(3)).
subtopics.example: Jordan, an analyst at an investor group, reads that a former audit partner who left practice three years ago may become PCAOB chair. Jordan notes that a CPA chair must have been out of practice for at least five years under Section 101(e)(2), and adds the point to the group's comment letter to the SEC.

review: Compare each member's CPA history with the two-CPA limit
Trace each member's term dates against the five-year, two-term limits
evidence: SEC press releases announcing each appointment, with start and end dates
Member biographies showing CPA licensing and practice history
audit_focus.recommend: Have the policy team cite Section 101(e) whenever it comments on a Board nominee.
audit_focus.decides: The SEC, as appointing authority, decides who fills each Board seat

subtopics.isaca_rule: Five full-time members, two and only two of whom are or have been CPAs; five-year staggered terms, two terms at most; appointed by the SEC after consulting the Federal Reserve chair and the Treasury Secretary.

exam_traps.trap: Most PCAOB members must be CPAs, since the Board oversees auditors.
exam_traps.why: Section 101(e)(2) caps CPA members at two of five, so non-CPAs always hold the majority.

exam_traps.trap: The President appoints PCAOB members with Senate confirmation.
exam_traps.why: Section 101(e)(4) gives appointment to the SEC, after it consults the Federal Reserve chair and the Treasury Secretary.

key_terms.definition: An accountant licensed by a U.S. state; the limit counts members who are or ever were licensed.
Terms that end in different years, so the whole Board never turns over at once.

subtopics.name: Funding Through Accounting Support Fees
subtopics.definition: The PCAOB is funded mainly by an annual accounting support fee paid by issuers in proportion to market capitalization, under a budget the SEC approves (Section 109).
subtopics.why_it_matters: Funding from issuers, rather than from audit firms or taxes, keeps the Board independent of the firms it inspects and of yearly appropriations.
how_it_works: The Board sets a yearly budget, and the SEC must approve it (Section 109(b)).
Each issuer's share is its average monthly equity market capitalization over the prior 12 months, divided by the total for all issuers (Section 109(g)).
Since Dodd-Frank, brokers and dealers also pay a share, in proportion to net capital (15 U.S.C. 7219(h), as amended in 2010).
The fees are not public money, and the Board does not depend on congressional appropriations (Section 109(c)(1) and its rule of construction).
Money penalties the Board collects fund merit scholarships for accounting students (Section 109(c)(2)).
Audit firms pay only registration and annual fees that recover processing costs (Section 102(f)).
subtopics.example: Ana, a policy analyst at a pension fund, reads that the PCAOB's next budget includes a large technology project. Ana notes that the SEC must approve the Board's budget under Section 109(b), so the fund sends its concerns to the SEC during that review instead of writing to the audit firms the Board inspects.

review: Trace the accounting support fee invoice to the Section 109 allocation basis
Compare the fee's market capitalization input with the issuer's own data
evidence: Accounting support fee invoice showing the allocation inputs
Exchange price and outstanding-share records used to recompute the capitalization input
audit_focus.recommend: Have the finance team record the fee as the issuer's regulatory cost, not as an audit fee.
audit_focus.decides: The Board assesses the fee under a budget the SEC approves

subtopics.isaca_rule: Issuers (and, since 2010, brokers and dealers) fund the PCAOB through accounting support fees, each issuer's share set by equity market capitalization, under a budget the SEC approves. Not taxes, and not audit firm dues.

exam_traps.trap: Audit firms fund the PCAOB through their dues.
exam_traps.why: Firms pay only registration and annual fees that recover processing costs. The Board's budget is recovered from accounting support fees (Section 109(c) and (d)).

exam_traps.trap: Congress funds the Board through yearly appropriations.
exam_traps.why: Section 109 says the fees are not public money and the Board is not subject to congressional appropriation procedures.

key_terms.definition: The annual fee issuers (and, since 2010, brokers and dealers) pay to fund the PCAOB and the recognized accounting standard setter.
The market value of a company's shares; Section 109 uses the monthly average over 12 months.

subtopics.name: SEC Oversight of the Board
subtopics.definition: Section 107 gives the SEC oversight and enforcement authority over the PCAOB: it approves Board rules, reviews Board sanctions, and can censure or limit the Board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The SEC is the PCAOB's regulator. Items that reverse the two roles, or let the Board act without SEC review, are testing this section.
how_it_works: No Board rule takes effect without prior SEC approval (Section 107(b)(2)).
The Board files notice of each final sanction, and the SEC may enhance, modify, cancel or reduce it (Section 107(c)).
Applying to the SEC for review of a Board sanction stays it, unless the SEC orders otherwise (Section 105(e)).
The SEC may relieve the Board of enforcement duties, censure it, or limit its activities after notice and a hearing (Section 107(d)).
The SEC can censure or remove Board members; Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010) struck the for-cause limits, so removal is at will (Sections 101(e)(6), 107(d)(3)).
subtopics.example: A shareholder group thinks a PCAOB fine on an audit firm was too light. Dana, its advocate, learns that the SEC, not a court, first reviews final Board sanctions and may enhance, reduce or cancel them under Section 107(c)(3), and explains this in the group's member newsletter.

review: Trace each PCAOB sanction cited internally to its SEC review status
Compare SEC orders on Board sanctions with the original Board order
evidence: SEC orders reviewing or modifying Board sanctions
The Board's published disciplinary order, with its date and SEC review status
audit_focus.recommend: Have the legal team confirm whether a Board sanction is stayed or final before relying on it.
audit_focus.decides: The SEC, as the Board's overseer, confirms or changes sanctions

subtopics.isaca_rule: The SEC oversees the PCAOB: it approves Board rules before they take effect, reviews and can change Board sanctions, and can censure or limit the Board and its members.

exam_traps.trap: PCAOB sanctions are final once the Board imposes them.
exam_traps.why: The SEC reviews final Board sanctions and may enhance, modify, cancel or reduce them; applying for review stays the sanction unless the SEC orders otherwise.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB oversees the SEC's enforcement work on auditors.
exam_traps.why: The relationship runs the other way: Section 107 gives the SEC oversight and enforcement authority over the Board.

key_terms.definition: A pause that keeps a sanction from taking effect while a review is pending.
A formal reprimand; the Board can censure firms, and the SEC can censure the Board.

topics.overview: Section 102 makes PCAOB registration mandatory for any firm that prepares, issues or takes part in an issuer's audit report. Section 106 applies the same rules to foreign firms and requires access to their workpapers, and Section 104(i) adds consequences for issuers whose auditors sit where inspections are blocked.
can_do: State who must register with the PCAOB and when
Explain what a registered firm consents to when it registers
Describe the work paper duties of foreign firms and of the U.S. firms that rely on them
Explain the trading ban for issuers whose auditors the PCAOB cannot inspect

subtopics.name: Mandatory Registration With the Board
subtopics.definition: Section 102 makes it unlawful for a firm that is not registered with the PCAOB to prepare, issue or take part in preparing an audit report for an issuer.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Registration is the gateway to the Board's other powers. A registered firm consents to cooperate with the Board, and an unregistered firm cannot audit issuers at all.
how_it_works: The duty covers preparing or issuing an audit report and participating in its preparation (Section 102(a)); since 2010 it also covers audits of brokers and dealers.
The application lists issuer clients, fees by type of service, quality control policies, licensed accountants and pending proceedings (Section 102(b)(2)).
The firm consents to give testimony and documents the Board requests, and secures the same consent from its people (Section 102(b)(3)).
The Board acts on a completed application within 45 days; a disapproval counts as a disciplinary sanction (Section 102(c)).
Registered firms file annual reports with the Board and pay registration and annual fees (Section 102(d) and (f)).
subtopics.example: Nadia, the risk partner at a registered firm, learns that a state court has opened a civil case naming one of the firm's audit partners over an issuer audit. Nadia makes sure the case is reported to the Board as its reporting rules require, because pending proceedings are part of the firm's registration information under Section 102(b)(2).

review: Confirm the firm's PCAOB registration before issuer audit work starts
Compare the issuer client list with the firm's latest annual report
evidence: The firm's entry in the Board's public registry, dated before fieldwork
Latest yearly filing the firm made to the Board, with its client list
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee confirm the auditor's PCAOB registration before engaging it for an issuer audit.
audit_focus.decides: The Board approves or disapproves a completed registration application

subtopics.isaca_rule: No registration, no issuer audit: under Section 102 an unregistered firm may not prepare, issue or participate in an issuer's audit report. Registering means consenting to the Board's requests for testimony and documents.

exam_traps.trap: A firm may start an issuer audit and register before the report is signed.
exam_traps.why: Section 102(a) bars an unregistered firm from even participating in preparing the report, so registration comes first.

exam_traps.trap: Registration is optional for small firms with few issuer clients.
exam_traps.why: Section 102 has no size exception for issuer auditors; size changes only how often the Board inspects under Section 104.

key_terms.definition: A company with securities registered with the SEC, required to file Exchange Act reports, or with a pending registration statement (Section 2(a)(7)).
The auditor's report on financial statements filed with the SEC, which only registered firms may prepare for issuers.

subtopics.name: Foreign Public Accounting Firms
subtopics.definition: A foreign accounting firm that prepares or furnishes an issuer's audit report is subject to the Act and to Board and SEC rules like a U.S. firm (Section 106).
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many issuers have operations or auditors abroad. Without access to foreign workpapers, U.S. regulators could not check audits that investors rely on.
how_it_works: Foreign firms that audit issuers must register and follow Board rules, in the same manner as U.S. firms (Section 106(a)(1)).
The Board may require registration of a foreign firm that plays a substantial role in an issuer's audit (Section 106(a)(2)).
A foreign firm whose work a registered firm relies on must produce its workpapers when the SEC or Board asks (15 U.S.C. 7216(b)(1)).
That foreign firm must also name an agent in the United States for SEC and Board requests (15 U.S.C. 7216(d)(2)).
The registered firm that relies on it must also produce those papers, and secure the foreign firm's agreement as a condition of reliance (15 U.S.C. 7216(b)(2)).
A willful refusal to comply violates the Act; the SEC, or the Board with SEC approval, may grant exemptions (15 U.S.C. 7216(c) and (e)).
subtopics.example: Before relying on a Lisbon firm's audit of an issuer's Portuguese unit, Sam, the group engagement partner at a registered U.S. firm, asks the Lisbon firm to sign a written, irrevocable consent naming Sam's firm as its agent for SEC and Board requests under 15 U.S.C. 7216(d)(1), and files it with the engagement records.

review: Trace each foreign firm the group audit relies on to a signed consent
Compare the list of component auditors with Board registration records
evidence: Signed irrevocable consents and powers of attorney from foreign firms
Board registration records for foreign firms that issue reports
audit_focus.recommend: Have the group engagement leaders secure a production agreement from every relied-on foreign firm before using its work.
audit_focus.decides: Exemptions come only from the SEC, or from the Board once the SEC agrees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Foreign firms that audit issuers are treated like U.S. firms. A registered firm that relies on a foreign firm's work must be able to produce that firm's workpapers when the SEC or the Board asks.

exam_traps.trap: Foreign audit firms are outside the PCAOB's reach because home-country regulators supervise them.
exam_traps.why: Section 106 subjects foreign firms that audit issuers to the Act and Board rules in the same manner as U.S. firms.

key_terms.definition: An accounting firm organized and operating under the laws of a foreign government (15 U.S.C. 7216(g)).
A person or firm named to receive regulators' requests and legal papers on another firm's behalf.

subtopics.name: Jurisdictions That Block Inspections
subtopics.definition: Section 104(i), added in 2020, requires the SEC to bar trading in an issuer whose auditor's foreign office the PCAOB cannot inspect for two consecutive years.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Some foreign authorities block PCAOB inspections. The rule puts the consequence on the issuer, so investors are not left relying on audits no regulator can check.
how_it_works: The Board determines that it cannot fully inspect or investigate an office because of a position a foreign authority takes (15 U.S.C. 7214(i)(2)(A)).
The SEC identifies each covered issuer that uses such an office for its audit report (15 U.S.C. 7214(i)(2)(A)).
An identified issuer must show the SEC that a government entity in that jurisdiction does not own or control it (15 U.S.C. 7214(i)(2)(B)).
After two consecutive non-inspection years the SEC must prohibit trading in the issuer's securities; a 2022 amendment cut this from three years (15 U.S.C. 7214(i)(3)).
The ban ends when the issuer certifies it has retained a firm the Board has inspected to the SEC's satisfaction (15 U.S.C. 7214(i)(3)(B)).
subtopics.example: A listed apparel issuer uses an audit office the SEC has flagged as one the PCAOB cannot inspect. Wei, its general counsel, prepares the government-ownership documentation the SEC requires and briefs the audit committee on engaging a firm the Board can inspect before a second flagged year arrives.

review: Confirm whether the SEC has identified the issuer under Section 104(i)
Trace the audit report to the auditor office and its inspection status
evidence: SEC published identification of the issuer, with each fiscal year covered
Board's published findings by jurisdiction, matched to the auditor's office location
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee plan an auditor change before a second consecutive non-inspection year.
audit_focus.decides: The Board determines which offices it cannot inspect; the SEC identifies issuers

subtopics.isaca_rule: If a foreign authority keeps the PCAOB from inspecting the auditor's office, the SEC identifies the issuer, and two consecutive identified years bring a mandatory trading ban.

exam_traps.trap: A non-inspectable auditor triggers only a disclosure, never a trading ban.
exam_traps.why: Section 104(i)(3) requires the SEC to prohibit trading after two consecutive non-inspection years.

key_terms.definition: A year, beginning after December 18, 2020, in which the SEC identifies the issuer for every covered report it files.
An issuer required to file reports under Exchange Act Section 13 or 15(d) (15 U.S.C. 7214(i)(1)(A)).

subtopics.name: Registration Decisions and Public Records
subtopics.definition: Section 102 sets how the PCAOB acts on a registration application, treats a refusal as a disciplinary sanction, and opens registration filings to the public, minus proprietary parts.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A refused firm cannot audit issuers, so the Act gives it the protections that come with a sanction. Public filings show who audits whom without exposing a firm's trade secrets.
how_it_works: The Board approves a completed application within 45 days unless it first issues a written disapproval or asks for more information (Section 102(c)(1), opened 31 Oct 2026).
A written disapproval counts as a disciplinary sanction under Sections 105(d) and 107(c), so it is reported and the SEC can review it (Section 102(c)(2)).
Each registered firm files an annual report with the Board, and more often if required, to update its registration information (Section 102(d)).
Applications and annual reports are open to public inspection, subject to Board and SEC rules and confidentiality laws (Section 102(e)).
In all events, the Board must protect information the firm reasonably identifies as proprietary (Section 102(e)).
subtopics.example: Rosa, the risk partner at a mid-sized firm preparing its first PCAOB filing, reviews which internal methodology guides to include. Rosa labels each guide with a short reason for confidential treatment and briefs the managing partner on the routes open if the Board turns the filing down.

review: Inspect the Board's public registry entry against the firm's own filing copy
Confirm each confidential marking in the filing carries a stated reason
evidence: Board registration decision letters and any written disapproval notice
Firm's annual report to the Board, with confidential sections marked
audit_focus.recommend: Have the firm's registration team document the basis for every confidentiality claim before filing.
audit_focus.decides: The Board decides applications; the SEC may review any disapproval as a sanction

subtopics.isaca_rule: A refused registration is treated as a disciplinary sanction, so the SEC can review it. Registration filings are public, but the Board must protect what the firm reasonably identifies as proprietary.

exam_traps.trap: A PCAOB refusal to register a firm is final; the SEC plays no part.
exam_traps.why: Section 102(c)(2) treats a written disapproval as a disciplinary sanction, which brings in SEC review under Section 107(c).

exam_traps.trap: Everything in a registration application is published.
exam_traps.why: Section 102(e) opens filings to public inspection but requires the Board to protect information the firm reasonably identifies as proprietary.

key_terms.definition: The Board's written refusal of a completed registration application, treated as a disciplinary sanction.
Confidential business information, such as internal methods, that a firm reasonably flags for protection from public disclosure.

subtopics.name: Substantial-Role Firms, Exemptions and Alternate Production
subtopics.definition: Section 106 lets the Board reach foreign firms that shape issuer audits without signing reports, lets U.S. authorities exempt foreign firms, and lets staff accept papers through other channels.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Group audits rely on firms abroad, and foreign laws can block transfers of papers. These tools keep U.S. oversight on the work investors rely on while allowing for real conflicts of law.
how_it_works: The Board may determine, by rule, that a foreign firm issuing no audit reports plays such a substantial role that it must register and accept oversight (Section 106(a)(2)).
The SEC, and the Board with SEC approval, may exempt any foreign firm or class of firms from the Act or its rules, with or without conditions (Section 106(c)).
Staff may let a foreign firm produce through alternate means, such as foreign counterpart regulators (15 U.S.C. 7216(f), added in 2010, opened 31 Oct 2026).
A willful refusal to comply with an SEC or Board request under Section 106 is a violation of the Act (15 U.S.C. 7216(e)).
subtopics.example: Ana, the compliance head at a registered firm, plans the group audit of an issuer with plants in three countries. One component firm abroad cannot ship its files under local secrecy law, so Ana raises with PCAOB staff, before fieldwork, whether that country's audit regulator can act as the channel.

review: Map each component firm abroad to its PCAOB registration status
Inspect correspondence agreeing any alternate production route with SEC or Board staff
evidence: Board rules or orders naming substantial-role firms
Written SEC or Board exemption orders covering foreign firms
audit_focus.recommend: Have the group engagement team settle the production route for each foreign component before relying on its work.
audit_focus.decides: The Board sets substantial-role rules; the SEC, or the Board with its approval, grants exemptions

subtopics.isaca_rule: Signing an issuer's audit report means registering; a substantial role can mean registering by Board rule. Only the SEC, or the Board with SEC approval, exempts foreign firms, and staff may accept papers through foreign regulators.

exam_traps.trap: A foreign firm that signs no audit report is beyond the PCAOB's reach.
exam_traps.why: Section 106(a)(2) lets the Board require a substantial-role firm to register, and Section 106(b) reaches the workpapers of firms whose material work is relied on.

exam_traps.trap: Foreign secrecy law excuses a foreign firm from producing workpapers.
exam_traps.why: The duty stays; Section 106(f) lets staff accept another route, such as a foreign counterpart, and a willful refusal violates the Act.

key_terms.definition: Work on issuer audits significant enough that the Board, by rule, treats the foreign firm as needing registration.
A route other than direct delivery, such as a foreign regulator, that staff may accept for producing papers.

topics.overview: The PCAOB sets the auditing, quality control, ethics and independence standards for issuer audits (Section 103), inspects registered firms on a schedule set by client count (Section 104), and investigates and disciplines firms and their associated persons (Section 105).
can_do: List the requirements Section 103 writes directly into the auditing standards
Apply the inspection frequency rule to a firm's issuer client count
Tell which sanctions need intentional, knowing or repeated conduct
Explain who the Board can discipline and what a bar means for issuers

subtopics.name: Standards the Board Must Set
subtopics.definition: Section 103 directs the PCAOB to set, by rule, the auditing, attestation, quality control, ethics and independence standards registered firms use for issuer audit reports.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These standards replaced profession-made rules for public company audits, and Section 103 writes a few requirements straight into the law, which are common exam targets.
how_it_works: The Board may adopt standards proposed by professional or advisory groups, but keeps full power to amend or repeal them (Section 103(a)(3)).
Firms must prepare and keep audit workpapers for at least seven years, in enough detail to support the report (Section 103(a)(2)(A)(i)).
Each report needs concurring or second-partner review and approval by a qualified person other than the person in charge, or an independent reviewer (Section 103(a)(2)(A)(ii)).
Each issuer audit report describes the scope of internal control testing under Section 404(b) and presents findings and material weaknesses (Section 103(a)(2)(A)(iii)).
Quality control standards cover independence monitoring, consultation, supervision, hiring, client acceptance and internal inspection (Section 103(a)(2)(B)).
subtopics.example: Kai, the methodology lead at a mid-size registered firm, reviews a draft integrated audit report for an issuer. Kai checks that it describes the scope of the firm's internal control testing and lists the material weakness the team found, as Section 103(a)(2)(A)(iii) requires, before sending it on for release.

review: Compare the firm's methodology manual with each Section 103 requirement
Check issuer engagements for evidence of second-partner approval
evidence: Signed concurring review approvals in engagement files
Archive and purge logs for issuer engagement files, with dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the firm's quality leaders map each Section 103 requirement to a methodology step and an owner.
audit_focus.decides: The Board sets the standards, subject to SEC approval

subtopics.isaca_rule: The PCAOB sets auditing, quality control, ethics and independence standards for issuer audits. The Act itself requires seven-year work paper retention, second-partner review and a description of internal control testing.

exam_traps.trap: Audit workpapers need be kept only five years, as Section 802 says.
exam_traps.why: Section 802 (18 U.S.C. 1520(a)(1)) sets five years, but Section 103 and Rule 2-06, made under 1520(a)(2), require seven; a knowing and willful breach of the rule is also a crime.

key_terms.definition: Review and approval of the audit report by a qualified partner who is not in charge of the audit.
The records of procedures, evidence and conclusions that support the auditor's report.

subtopics.name: Inspections of Registered Firms
subtopics.definition: Section 104 requires the PCAOB to run a continuing program of inspections of registered firms, checking compliance with the Act, rules and professional standards on issuer audits.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Inspections replaced self-regulation for public company auditors. How often a firm is inspected depends on how many issuers it audits, a number exam items like to reverse.
how_it_works: Firms that regularly issue audit reports for more than 100 issuers are inspected every year (Section 104(b)(1)(A)).
Firms with 100 or fewer issuer clients are inspected at least once every three years (Section 104(b)(1)(B)).
The Board may adjust schedules by rule and hold special inspections on its own motion or at the SEC's request (Section 104(b)(2)).
Inspectors review selected engagements, evaluate the firm's quality control system and test its procedures (Section 104(d)).
Reports go to the SEC and state regulators; quality control criticisms stay private if fixed to the Board's satisfaction within 12 months (Section 104(g)).
A firm that answered the draft report and disagrees with the final one may seek SEC review within 30 days (Section 104(f) and (h)).
subtopics.example: After an inspection, the Board's draft report criticizes how a firm monitors independence. Imani, the firm's managing partner, sends a written response, which the Board attaches to the final report, and starts a remediation plan so the criticism can be addressed within 12 months under Section 104(g).

review: Compare the firm's issuer client count with the inspection frequency threshold
Test whether fixes for each quality control finding were finished on schedule
evidence: Public portion of the Board's report and the firm's reply letter
Remediation plan and Board letters on quality control criticisms
audit_focus.recommend: Have the firm's leaders fix quality control criticisms and document the fixes within the 12-month window.
audit_focus.decides: The Board decides whether criticisms were addressed to its satisfaction

subtopics.isaca_rule: More than 100 issuer clients: inspected every year. 100 or fewer: at least once every three years. The PCAOB inspects audit firms, not issuers, and the SEC can ask for special inspections.

exam_traps.trap: The SEC inspects audit firms; the PCAOB only writes standards.
exam_traps.why: Section 104 gives the inspection program to the Board. The SEC oversees the Board and may request special inspections.

exam_traps.trap: Small firms are inspected yearly and large firms every three years.
exam_traps.why: Reversed: firms auditing more than 100 issuers are inspected yearly; firms with 100 or fewer, at least every three years.

key_terms.definition: An extra inspection the Board starts on its own motion or at the SEC's request.
A firm's policies for independence, supervision, consultation, hiring, client acceptance and internal inspection.

subtopics.name: Investigations and Discipline
subtopics.definition: Section 105 lets the PCAOB investigate registered firms and their associated persons and, after fair procedures, impose sanctions ranging from censure to revoking registration.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Discipline gives inspections teeth. Exam items test who can be disciplined, and which sanctions need intentional or repeated misconduct.
how_it_works: The Board can require testimony and documents from firms and their people, and seek SEC subpoenas for others (Section 105(b)(2)).
Refusing to cooperate can bring a suspension, a bar or revocation of registration (Section 105(b)(3)).
Sanctions include censure, training, money penalties, activity limits, bars, and suspension or revocation of registration (Section 105(c)(4)).
Revocation, bars, activity limits and the higher money penalties need intentional or knowing conduct, including recklessness, or repeated negligence (Section 105(c)(5)).
Hearings are private unless the Board orders otherwise with the parties' consent; sanctions are reported to the SEC, state regulators and the public (Section 105(c)(2) and (d)).
Firms and supervisors can be sanctioned for failing to reasonably supervise someone who breaks the rules (Section 105(c)(6)).
subtopics.example: During a Board investigation, a registered firm's former audit manager refuses to testify. Lucia, the firm's general counsel, explains that noncooperation can lead the Board to bar the manager from association with any registered firm under Section 105(b)(3), and logs the refusal in the firm's record of Board requests.

review: Compare each sanction with the conduct finding behind it
Trace Board requests for documents to the firm's responses and dates
evidence: Board disciplinary orders with their supporting statements
Firm log of Board document and testimony requests
audit_focus.recommend: Have the firm's leaders answer every Board request fully and on time, since noncooperation is itself sanctionable.
audit_focus.decides: The Board imposes sanctions, subject to SEC review

subtopics.isaca_rule: The PCAOB disciplines registered firms and their associated persons, not issuers. The heaviest sanctions need intentional, knowing or reckless conduct, or repeated negligence; a single negligent act allows only the lesser sanctions.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB can fine an issuer's CFO for misstated financial statements.
exam_traps.why: Section 105 reaches registered firms and their associated persons. Issuer officers answer to the SEC and the courts.

exam_traps.trap: One negligent audit can lead to revocation of a firm's registration.
exam_traps.why: Section 105(c)(5) limits revocation, bars, activity limits and the higher penalties to intentional or knowing conduct, including recklessness, or repeated negligence.

key_terms.definition: A sanction that stops a person from associating with any registered public accounting firm, for a time or permanently.
A firm's or supervisor's failure to reasonably oversee someone who then breaks the rules.

subtopics.name: Effect of a Suspension or Bar
subtopics.definition: A PCAOB suspension or bar stops a person from working with any registered firm and, without Board or SEC consent, from accounting or financial management roles at issuers.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A bar would mean little if a barred auditor could move into a client's finance team. Section 105(c)(7) closes that door and binds the hiring issuer too.
how_it_works: A suspended or barred person may not willfully become or stay associated with any registered firm without Board or SEC consent (Section 105(c)(7)(A)).
A registered firm that knew, or should have known, of the bar may not permit that association (Section 105(c)(7)(A)).
The same person may not willfully take an accountancy or financial management role at an issuer, broker or dealer (15 U.S.C. 7215(c)(7)(B)).
An issuer that knew, or should have known, of the bar may not permit that role without Board or SEC consent (wording as amended in 2010).
Only the Board or the SEC can consent; the issuer's own board or audit committee cannot.
subtopics.example: A regional bank holding company that files with the SEC shortlists Ravi for assistant treasurer. A background check shows a PCAOB order barring Ravi from association with registered firms. Hana, the bank's general counsel, pauses the offer and briefs the hiring manager on the legal risk to the bank.

review: Screen finance and accounting candidates against PCAOB disciplinary orders
Compare current finance staff names with published Board bars and suspensions
evidence: Search results from the PCAOB's published disciplinary orders
Written Board or SEC consent on file for any barred or suspended finance employee
audit_focus.recommend: Have human resources and the general counsel check PCAOB bars before any finance or accounting hire.
audit_focus.decides: The Board or the SEC decides whether to consent to the association

subtopics.isaca_rule: A PCAOB bar follows the person: no registered firm, and no accountancy or financial management role at an issuer, without Board or SEC consent. An issuer that knew or should have known of the bar breaks the law by allowing it.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB regulates only audit firms, so an issuer may hire anyone the Board has barred.
exam_traps.why: Section 105(c)(7)(B) makes it unlawful for an issuer that knew or should have known of the bar to permit such a role without Board or SEC consent.

exam_traps.trap: The audit committee can approve hiring a barred former auditor.
exam_traps.why: The Act names only the Board or the SEC as able to consent.

key_terms.definition: A sanction, temporary or permanent, that stops a person from associating with registered firms (Section 105(c)(4)(B)).
A role at an issuer, broker or dealer that involves its accounting, financial reporting or management of its finances.

subtopics.name: Failure to Supervise
subtopics.definition: Section 105(c)(6) lets the Board sanction a registered firm or its supervisors for failing reasonably to supervise a rule breaker, with a safe harbor for sound procedures.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Audit work is done by teams. The rule holds firms and supervisors to account for weak oversight, while protecting supervisors who follow sound procedures in good faith.
how_it_works: The Board may sanction the firm or a supervisory person when both findings below are made (15 U.S.C. 7215(c)(6)(A), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Two findings are needed: the firm failed reasonably to supervise an associated person, and that person then broke the Act, Board rules, securities laws or professional standards.
The safe harbor first needs firm procedures and a system that comply with Board rules and would reasonably prevent and detect the violation (Section 105(c)(6)(B)).
It also needs the supervisor to have reasonably carried out those procedures, with no reasonable cause to believe they were not being followed.
Dodd-Frank Section 929F(h) added former supervisors; the Board's wider reach to former associated persons is in 4C3 (notes to 15 U.S.C. 7215, opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: An inspection finds that a senior associate skipped inventory steps on one issuer audit. Kofi, the firm's head of quality, prepares a timeline for the Board showing who oversaw the associate, what they looked at and why nothing signaled the gap.

review: Trace supervisory sign-offs on the engagement to the firm's written review procedures
Compare the firm's supervision policies with Board quality control rules
evidence: Signed engagement review checklists and supervision logs
Training and acknowledgment records for the firm's supervision procedures
audit_focus.recommend: Have the firm's quality leaders document each supervisor's review steps so the safe harbor can be shown.
audit_focus.decides: The Board decides whether supervision failed, subject to SEC review

subtopics.isaca_rule: A firm or supervisor can be sanctioned for failing reasonably to supervise someone who breaks the rules, but not if compliant procedures existed and the supervisor reasonably followed them without cause for suspicion.

exam_traps.trap: A supervisor is automatically sanctioned whenever a team member breaks the rules.
exam_traps.why: Section 105(c)(6) requires a failure reasonably to supervise, and its safe harbor protects supervisors who reasonably followed compliant procedures.

exam_traps.trap: Written procedures alone protect a supervisor.
exam_traps.why: The safe harbor needs both compliant procedures that would reasonably prevent and detect the violation and a supervisor who reasonably carried them out with no reasonable cause to think they were being ignored.

key_terms.definition: Someone at a registered firm responsible for overseeing the work of an associated person.
A set of conditions that, when met, means a person is not treated as having broken a rule.

topics.overview: Accounting principles come from a private standard setter the SEC recognizes under Section 108, which is FASB; the PCAOB writes auditing standards. Section 107 makes every PCAOB rule wait for SEC approval, and the JOBS Act keeps some PCAOB rules away from emerging growth company audits.
can_do: Tell which body sets accounting standards and which sets auditing standards for issuers
Explain when a new PCAOB rule or standard takes effect
Decide whether a new PCAOB rule applies to an emerging growth company's audit
Explain how the Board adopts standards drafted by professional and advisory groups

subtopics.name: Recognized Accounting Standard Setters
subtopics.definition: Section 108 lets the SEC recognize, as generally accepted, the accounting principles of a private standard setter that meets set criteria; the SEC recognized FASB in 2003.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The PCAOB sets auditing standards, not accounting standards. Mixing up the two bodies is one of the most common errors in this domain.
how_it_works: The standard setter must be private, with a board of trustees mostly free of recent ties to registered firms (Section 108(a), adding Securities Act Section 19(b)).
It must be funded under Section 109 and able to act promptly on emerging accounting issues (Section 108(a)).
In Release No. 33-8221 (2003) the SEC found FASB met the criteria, so FASB standards are generally accepted under the securities laws.
The SEC keeps its own power to set accounting principles (Section 108(c)).
Issuers fund the recognized standard setter through an accounting support fee as well (Section 109(a) and (e)).
Section 108(d) had the SEC study a principles-based accounting system and report to Congress within one year (15 U.S.C. 7218(d), opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: Tomas, a controller at a regional bank, asks why the bank's accounting support fees cover a standard setter it never hired. Tomas learns that Section 109 funds the SEC-recognized standard setter, FASB, through issuer fees, and records both the PCAOB and FASB amounts as regulatory costs.

review: Compare disclosures that name accounting standards with the recognized standard setter
Trace policy references to FASB and PCAOB standards to the right body
evidence: Release No. 33-8221 text, checked against the standards the manual cites
Accounting policy manual citing the standards followed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the controller's team cite FASB for accounting and the PCAOB only for auditing standards in disclosures.
audit_focus.decides: The SEC grants recognition; issuer management follows those principles in its statements

subtopics.isaca_rule: Accounting standards come from a private standard setter the SEC recognizes under Section 108 (FASB, since 2003); auditing standards for issuer audits come from the PCAOB. The SEC keeps final authority over both.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB sets accounting standards for issuers.
exam_traps.why: The PCAOB sets auditing and related standards for registered firms. Accounting principles come from the SEC-recognized standard setter, FASB.

key_terms.definition: The Financial Accounting Standards Board, the private body whose standards the SEC recognizes as generally accepted.
The accounting rules companies follow when preparing financial statements filed with the SEC.

subtopics.name: How a PCAOB Rule Takes Effect
subtopics.definition: Under Section 107(b), no PCAOB rule or standard takes effect until the SEC approves it, after publishing notice and inviting public comment.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Firms and issuers must know when a new standard binds them. A standard the Board has adopted but the SEC has not approved is not yet in force.
how_it_works: The Board adopts a proposed rule or standard and files it with the SEC (Section 107(b)).
The SEC handles proposals under Exchange Act Section 19(b) as if the Board were a registered securities association: notice, comment, then a decision (Section 107(b)(4)).
The SEC approves a rule consistent with the Act and securities laws, or necessary or appropriate for the public interest or investor protection (Section 107(b)(3)).
No Board rule takes effect without prior SEC approval (Section 107(b)(2)); the SEC may also delete from or add to Board rules (Section 107(b)(5)).
Independence rules that implement Title II are Board rules too, with the same approval step (Section 103(b)).
subtopics.example: Mara, the governance lead at a public pension fund, reads that the SEC has published notice of a PCAOB standard on audit firm reporting. Mara files a comment letter with the SEC during the notice period, since the standard cannot take effect until the SEC approves it.

review: Confirm SEC approval and the effective date before applying a new standard
Compare the firm's standards tracker with SEC approval orders
evidence: Commission approval order, with its release number and effective date
Federal Register notice of the proposed rule
audit_focus.recommend: Have the firm's methodology team apply a new Board standard only from the effective date the SEC approved.
audit_focus.decides: The SEC holds final say; a Board vote alone does not make a rule binding

subtopics.isaca_rule: The PCAOB adopts, the SEC approves, and only then does the rule take effect. The SEC can also change Board rules itself.

exam_traps.trap: A PCAOB standard is effective as soon as the Board adopts it.
exam_traps.why: Section 107(b)(2) says no Board rule takes effect without prior SEC approval.

key_terms.definition: Any proposed Board rule or change to one, which the SEC must approve before it takes effect (Section 107(b)(1)).
Publishing a proposal so the public can send written views before a decision is made.

subtopics.name: New PCAOB Rules and Emerging Growth Companies
subtopics.definition: Under Section 103(a)(3)(C), added by the JOBS Act in 2012, some PCAOB rules do not apply to audits of emerging growth companies (EGCs).
subtopics.why_it_matters: Whether a new standard applies can depend on the issuer's status. A scenario that names an emerging growth company may be testing this carve-out.
how_it_works: Board rules requiring mandatory audit firm rotation do not apply to EGC audits (15 U.S.C. 7213(a)(3)(C)).
Rules requiring an auditor discussion and analysis supplement to the audit report do not apply to EGC audits either.
Any other Board rule adopted after April 5, 2012 does not apply to EGC audits unless the SEC decides it should (15 U.S.C. 7213(a)(3)(C)).
The SEC decides after weighing investor protection and whether the rule promotes efficiency, competition and capital formation.
subtopics.example: Lucas, the controller of a newly public biotech that qualifies as an EGC, reads about a new PCAOB auditing requirement. Lucas asks the engagement partner whether the SEC decided it applies to EGC audits, since rules adopted after April 5, 2012 do not apply otherwise, and records the answer for the audit committee.

review: Confirm the issuer's EGC status for the period under audit
Inspect each new Board rule's SEC approval order for an EGC decision
evidence: SEC approval order stating whether the rule applies to EGC audits
Issuer filings stating its EGC status
audit_focus.recommend: Have management keep a register of Board standards adopted after April 5, 2012, noting whether SEC action extends each to EGC audits.
audit_focus.decides: Only an SEC determination extends a newer Board rule to growth-company audits

subtopics.isaca_rule: For an emerging growth company's audit, Board rules on mandatory firm rotation or auditor discussion and analysis never apply, and other rules adopted after April 5, 2012 apply only if the SEC so decides.

exam_traps.trap: Every PCAOB standard applies to every issuer audit.
exam_traps.why: Section 103(a)(3)(C) exempts EGC audits from firm rotation and auditor discussion and analysis rules, and from later rules unless the SEC decides otherwise.

key_terms.definition: A newly public issuer under a revenue cap that gets scaled requirements for a limited time under the JOBS Act.
A supplement to the audit report giving more detail on the audit and the financial statements.

subtopics.name: How the Board Builds Its Standards
subtopics.definition: Section 103 lets the PCAOB write its own standards or adopt ones proposed by professional or advisory groups, while keeping full control over everything it adopts.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Standard setting draws on the profession's expertise without handing it control. Exam items test who drafts, who decides and who may sit on the advisory groups.
how_it_works: The Board sets auditing, attestation, quality control, ethics and independence standards for registered firms by rule (Section 103(a)(1)).
It may adopt as its rules standards proposed by professional groups it designates or by its advisory groups, subject to Section 107 (Section 103(a)(3)(A)(i)).
It keeps full authority to modify, supplement, revise or repeal any adopted standard, in whole or in part (Section 103(a)(3)(A)(ii)).
Expert advisory groups may include practicing accountants and other experts, under Board conflict-of-interest rules, and recommend content, including drafts (Section 103(a)(4)).
The Board reports its standard-setting results and pending agenda in its annual report to the SEC (Section 103(d)).
subtopics.example: Hiroshi, a technical partner at a regional firm, is invited to join a PCAOB panel on going-concern reporting. Before accepting, Hiroshi asks the firm's general counsel to review the Board's conflict-of-interest requirements for advisers and lists the firm's issuer clients most affected by the topic.

review: Trace each adopted standard to its Board adoption and SEC approval records
Compare advisory group membership disclosures with the Board's conflict rules
evidence: Board adopting releases citing the group that proposed the text
Advisory panel meeting records and membership lists posted by the Board
audit_focus.recommend: Have the firm's methodology team track each standard's origin and later Board amendments in one register.
audit_focus.decides: The Board decides, subject to SEC approval; outside panels only advise

subtopics.isaca_rule: The Board may borrow drafts from professional groups and take advice from expert groups that include practicing accountants, but whatever it adopts becomes a Board rule, and the Board keeps full authority to amend or repeal it.

exam_traps.trap: A professional group that drafted a standard controls later changes to it.
exam_traps.why: Section 103(a)(3)(A)(ii) keeps full authority with the Board to modify or repeal any standard it adopted.

exam_traps.trap: Practicing accountants may not serve on PCAOB advisory groups.
exam_traps.why: Section 103(a)(4) expressly allows practicing accountants on expert advisory groups, subject to Board rules preventing conflicts of interest.

key_terms.definition: A group of accountants the Board designates or recognizes by rule as a source of proposed standards.
A panel the Board convenes to recommend the content of its standards, including drafts.

topics.overview: Section 201 bars an issuer's auditor from providing nine kinds of non-audit service during the audit. Section 202 makes the audit committee approve in advance every other service the auditor provides, including tax work, with a narrow de minimis exception.
can_do: Name the prohibited non-audit services and tell them from permitted ones
Explain who must preapprove auditor services and what may be delegated
Apply all three conditions of the de minimis exception

subtopics.name: Prohibited Non-Audit Services
subtopics.definition: Section 201 bars a registered firm from providing nine kinds of non-audit service to an issuer at the same time as it audits that issuer.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An auditor that keeps the books, builds the systems or runs internal audit would end up auditing its own work. The ban protects independence in fact and in appearance.
how_it_works: Bookkeeping and other services related to the accounting records or financial statements (Exchange Act Section 10A(g)(1)).
Financial information systems design and implementation; appraisal or valuation services, fairness opinions or contribution-in-kind reports; actuarial services (10A(g)(2) to (4)).
Internal audit outsourcing; management functions or human resources; broker or dealer, investment adviser or investment banking services (10A(g)(5) to (7)).
Legal services and expert services unrelated to the audit, and any other service the Board bans by regulation (10A(g)(8) and (9)).
SEC Rule 2-01(c)(4) gives the detail; several bans apply unless it is reasonable to conclude the results will not be subject to audit procedures.
The Board may grant case-by-case exemptions, subject to SEC review (Section 201(b)).
subtopics.example: Ama, the treasurer of a retailer, wants its audit firm to value a brand acquired in a merger because the firm already knows the business. The compliance team points out that valuation services are on Section 201's prohibited list for the issuer's auditor, and Ama hires a separate valuation firm.

review: Compare each auditor service in the fee ledger with the prohibited list
Inspect engagement letters for services in a banned category
evidence: Fee ledger by service type for the issuer's auditor
Auditor engagement letters for all non-audit work
audit_focus.recommend: Have management route any banned service to a different provider, and the audit committee confirm the split.
audit_focus.decides: The audit committee oversees auditor independence; the Board may grant exemptions

subtopics.isaca_rule: The issuer's auditor may not provide any of the nine prohibited non-audit services during the audit. Audit committee preapproval cannot cure a prohibited service; only a Board exemption can.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit outsourcing is allowed if the audit committee preapproves it.
exam_traps.why: Internal audit outsourcing is on the Section 201 list. Preapproval applies only to non-audit services that are not prohibited.

key_terms.definition: Any professional service a registered firm provides to an issuer other than in connection with an audit or review (Section 2(a)(8)).
At the same time the firm audits the issuer, which is when the Section 201 ban applies.

subtopics.name: Audit Committee Preapproval
subtopics.definition: Section 202 requires the issuer's audit committee to approve in advance all audit services and every permitted non-audit service, tax services included, that its auditor provides.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Preapproval puts the independent audit committee, not management, in control of what else the auditor does, so fees cannot quietly erode independence.
how_it_works: All audit services, comfort letters for underwritings included, and permitted non-audit services need the audit committee's advance approval (Exchange Act Section 10A(h) and (i)(1)(A)).
Tax services are not on the Section 201 list and need preapproval (10A(h)); PCAOB ethics rules (not opened) also restrict some tax services.
The committee may delegate preapproval to independent directors on the committee, whose decisions go to the full committee at each scheduled meeting (10A(i)(3)).
Preapproval policies must be detailed by service, keep the committee informed of each service, and never delegate its duties to management (17 CFR 210.2-01(c)(7)(i)(B)).
Approved non-audit services are disclosed to investors in periodic reports (10A(i)(2)).
subtopics.example: At its January meeting, a chemical issuer's audit committee approves a policy listing the specific tax compliance services its auditor may provide, up to a set budget. Noor, the committee chair, asks that each service used under the policy be reported at every meeting, so the committee is informed of each one.

review: Trace each auditor engagement to a dated audit committee preapproval
Read the delegation clause and confirm no executive holds approval power
evidence: Audit committee minutes recording preapprovals and delegate reports
Service-by-service fee caps in the committee's written policy
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee approve every auditor service in advance, directly or through a detailed policy.
audit_focus.decides: Approval power sits with the committee and its delegates, not executives

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every audit and permitted non-audit service by the issuer's auditor needs the audit committee's advance approval. The committee may delegate to its independent members, never to management.

exam_traps.trap: Management can preapprove routine auditor services to save the committee time.
exam_traps.why: Section 202 gives preapproval to the audit committee, and SEC Rule 2-01(c)(7) bars policies that delegate the committee's duties to management.

exam_traps.trap: Tax services are banned for the issuer's auditor.
exam_traps.why: Section 201 names tax services as non-audit services allowed with audit committee preapproval, though PCAOB ethics rules restrict some kinds of tax work.

key_terms.definition: Audit committee approval given before the auditor is engaged for a service.
An audit committee policy approving specific services in advance, with the committee told of each use.

subtopics.name: The De Minimis Exception
subtopics.definition: The de minimis exception waives advance approval for small non-audit services not recognized as non-audit when engaged, if the audit committee approves them before the audit ends.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is a narrow fix for honest oversights. All three conditions must hold, and it never covers a prohibited service.
how_it_works: All such non-audit services total no more than 5% of the revenues the issuer paid its auditor in that fiscal year (10A(i)(1)(B)(i)).
The issuer did not recognize them as non-audit services at the time of the engagement (10A(i)(1)(B)(ii)).
They are promptly brought to the audit committee and approved before the audit is completed, by the committee or a delegated member (10A(i)(1)(B)(iii)).
SEC Rule 2-01(c)(7)(i)(C) repeats the same three conditions.
subtopics.example: In its quarterly fee review, a logistics issuer's finance team finds that its auditor ran an unapproved advisory project whose fees equal 8% of what the issuer paid the auditor that year. Owen, the assistant controller, sees the exception cannot apply, and reports the lapse to the audit committee chair the same day.

review: Compute unapproved non-audit fees as a share of total auditor fees
Trace each unapproved service to committee approval before audit completion
evidence: Auditor fee schedule for the fiscal year by service
Audit committee minutes approving the service, with dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have management report any unapproved auditor service to the audit committee as soon as it is found.
audit_focus.decides: Committee members approve each late-found service; executives only report it

subtopics.isaca_rule: The de minimis waiver needs all three conditions: no more than 5% of the year's fees paid to the auditor, not recognized as non-audit at engagement, and prompt audit committee approval before the audit is completed.

exam_traps.trap: Any non-audit service under 5% of auditor fees needs no approval.
exam_traps.why: The 5% test is one of three conditions. The service must also have been unrecognized at engagement and approved by the committee before the audit ends.

key_terms.definition: Too small to matter; here, a narrow waiver of advance approval for small, unrecognized services.
Everything the issuer paid its auditor in the fiscal year, the base for the 5% test.

topics.topic_name: Partner rotation and auditor reports to the audit committee
topics.overview: Section 203 rotates the lead and reviewing audit partners after five consecutive years; the firm itself does not have to rotate. Section 204 makes the auditor report critical accounting policies, alternative treatments and other key written communications to the audit committee. SEC rules define which partners rotate and exempt the smallest firms while the PCAOB reviews their engagements.
can_do: Apply the partner rotation and time-out periods to an engagement history
Tell partner rotation from audit firm rotation
List what the auditor must report to the audit committee, and when
Decide which partners the SEC rotation rules cover, and when a small firm is exempt

subtopics.name: Audit Partner Rotation
subtopics.definition: Section 203 bars a registered firm from auditing an issuer if its lead or coordinating partner, or its reviewing partner, served in each of the issuer's five previous fiscal years.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Long tenure can breed familiarity. Rotation brings fresh eyes while the firm stays; exam items test who rotates and that firms do not have to.
how_it_works: The lead (or coordinating) audit partner and the partner who reviews the audit both rotate (Exchange Act Section 10A(j)).
Under SEC Rule 2-01(c)(6), lead partners and engagement quality reviewers serve at most five consecutive years, then sit out five years.
Other audit partners serve at most seven consecutive years, then sit out two years (17 CFR 210.2-01(c)(6)(i)).
Firms with under five issuer audit clients and under ten partners are exempt if the Board reviews those engagements at least every three years (210.2-01(c)(6)(ii)).
The Act rotates partners only; mandatory audit firm rotation was studied, not imposed (Section 207).
subtopics.example: At a medical device issuer, the audit firm proposes that the partner who led the last five audits serve as engagement quality reviewer on the next one. Farah, the audit committee chair, notes that the SEC rule's five-year time-out covers either role, and asks the firm to propose a different partner.

review: Trace each partner's years on the engagement from firm records
Compare lead and reviewer tenure with the five-year limit
evidence: Auditor's partner rotation schedule for the issuer
Engagement team listings by fiscal year
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee review the firm's rotation plan each year before the next audit is planned.
audit_focus.decides: The firm assigns partners; the audit committee oversees compliance

subtopics.isaca_rule: The lead and reviewing partners rotate after five consecutive years, with a five-year time-out under SEC rules; other audit partners rotate after seven. Partners rotate; the Act does not make the firm rotate.

exam_traps.trap: Section 203 requires issuers to change audit firms every five years.
exam_traps.why: Section 203 rotates partners. Firm rotation was only studied, by the Comptroller General under Section 207.

key_terms.definition: The audit partner with primary responsibility for the audit, also called the coordinating partner.
The partner who reviews the significant judgments and overall conclusion of the audit before release.
The period after rotation during which a partner may not return to that client's audit in a covered role.

subtopics.name: Auditor Reports to the Audit Committee
subtopics.definition: Section 204 requires the issuer's registered firm to report critical accounting policies, alternative GAAP treatments and other material written communications to the audit committee on time.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The audit committee oversees the auditor and the financial reporting process. It can weigh management's choices only if it hears what the auditor discussed and preferred.
how_it_works: Report all critical accounting policies and practices to be used (Exchange Act Section 10A(k)(1)).
Report alternative GAAP treatments discussed with management, their ramifications, and the treatment the firm prefers (10A(k)(2)).
Report other material written communications with management, such as the management letter or schedule of unadjusted differences (10A(k)(3)).
The SEC's adopting release adds examples such as reports on internal control observations and the engagement letter (Release No. 33-8183 Section II.G.3, opened 31 Oct 2026).
SEC Rule 2-07 requires these reports before the audit report is filed with the SEC (17 CFR 210.2-07(a)).
subtopics.example: Before an energy issuer files its annual report, the independent auditor gives the audit committee the schedule of unadjusted differences it sent to management. Chen, the committee secretary, files it with the minutes, and the chair asks management to explain each item it left uncorrected.

review: Compare auditor letters to management with those given to the committee
Confirm the auditor's report to the committee predates the filing
evidence: Meeting agenda pack and minutes logging receipt of each required item, with dates
Every letter the auditor sent management during the year, for completeness
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee chair require these reports, in writing, before the annual filing.
audit_focus.decides: The audit committee weighs the treatments; management prepares the statements

subtopics.isaca_rule: The auditor reports to the audit committee, not to the CFO: critical accounting policies, alternative GAAP treatments discussed with management with their ramifications and the firm's preference, and other material written communications, before filing.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor reports alternative treatments to the CFO, who decides what the committee sees.
exam_traps.why: Section 204 requires the firm to report directly to the audit committee, including the treatment the firm prefers.

key_terms.definition: An accounting policy central to the reported results, which the auditor must report to the committee.
The auditor's list of misstatements it found that management chose not to correct.
The auditor's written comments to management on matters found during the audit.

subtopics.name: Which Partners Count for Rotation
subtopics.definition: SEC rules apply partner rotation to audit partners, a defined group that leaves out partners who only consult the audit team on technical issues.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Rotation limits mean nothing until you know who they cover. Items test whether a role, such as a national office adviser, is an audit partner at all.
how_it_works: Audit partners include the lead partner and the Engagement Quality Reviewer (17 CFR 210.2-01(f)(7)(ii)(A) and (B), opened 31 Oct 2026).
They also include other team partners with more than ten hours on the consolidated statements (210.2-01(f)(7)(ii)(C), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Lead partners on subsidiaries with 20% or more of consolidated assets or revenues are audit partners too (210.2-01(f)(7)(ii)(D), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Partners who only consult the team on technical or industry-specific issues, such as national office partners, are excluded (210.2-01(f)(7)(ii); Release No. 33-8183 Section II.C.2).
Only audit partners are subject to the five-year and seven-year limits in Rule 2-01(c)(6) (opened 31 Oct 2026).
subtopics.example: Before planning starts at a listed shipping company, Tomasz, the audit committee chair, notes that a subsidiary now earns a quarter of group revenue. Tomasz asks the firm to add that subsidiary's lead partner to its rotation tracking and to report how long the partner has served there.

review: Compare the firm's audit partner list with the Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii) categories
Trace subsidiary lead partners to the 20% asset or revenue test
evidence: Firm's schedule of audit partners with consecutive years on the client
Subsidiary asset and revenue shares from the consolidation schedules
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee review the firm's audit partner classifications whenever subsidiary sizes shift.
audit_focus.decides: The firm classifies partners; the audit committee oversees its rotation compliance

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rotation reaches audit partners only: the lead partner, the quality reviewer, other decision-making partners with more than ten hours, and lead partners on 20% subsidiaries. Technical consultants, such as national office partners, are not audit partners.

exam_traps.trap: Every partner who works on an issuer's audit must rotate.
exam_traps.why: Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii) limits rotation to defined audit partners and excludes partners who only consult on technical or industry issues.

key_terms.definition: A partner on the audit team covered by SEC rotation rules, as defined in Rule 2-01(f)(7)(ii).
A firm's technical specialist consulted on accounting or auditing questions, outside the audit's decision-making team.

subtopics.name: Rotation Relief for Small Firms
subtopics.definition: SEC Rule 2-01(c)(6)(ii) exempts very small audit firms from partner rotation, but only while the PCAOB reviews the engagements that would otherwise breach the limits.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A firm with a handful of partners may have no one to rotate in. The SEC eased the rule for such firms but traded rotation for outside review, and items test that condition.
how_it_works: The exemption covers a firm with fewer than five issuer audit clients and fewer than ten partners (17 CFR 210.2-01(c)(6)(ii), opened 31 Oct 2026).
It holds only if the PCAOB reviews each engagement that would otherwise breach the rotation limits at least once every three years (210.2-01(c)(6)(ii)).
The SEC codified an earlier professional exemption and added the Board review to protect audit quality (Release No. 33-8183 Section II.C.4, opened 31 Oct 2026).
The release calls it a special review, focused on audit quality and the independence and competence of key engagement personnel.
Compare Rule 2-01(c)(8): the partner pay rule exempts firms of the same size with no review condition (see 2B3.5).
subtopics.example: Mei runs a small CPA practice with two public company clients. Before taking on a third, Mei sets a reminder to ask each client's audit committee chair when the PCAOB last examined that engagement, and records the answers.

review: Compare the firm's partner and issuer client counts with the exemption limits
Trace each engagement relying on the exemption to its latest Board review date
evidence: Firm's year-end headcount report and list of public audit clients
Board correspondence confirming the special review of each engagement
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee confirm each year that the Board review condition is still met before the partner continues.
audit_focus.decides: The firm claims the exemption; the Board's reviews keep it available

subtopics.isaca_rule: A firm with fewer than five issuer audit clients and fewer than ten partners is exempt from partner rotation only while the PCAOB reviews each affected engagement at least once every three years.

exam_traps.trap: Small firms are exempt from partner rotation outright.
exam_traps.why: Rule 2-01(c)(6)(ii) makes the exemption depend on a PCAOB review of each affected engagement at least once every three years.

exam_traps.trap: The audit committee can approve a partner's longer service instead.
exam_traps.why: Neither Section 203 nor Rule 2-01(c)(6) gives the audit committee power to extend a partner's service.

key_terms.definition: Relief from partner rotation for firms with fewer than five issuer audit clients and fewer than ten partners, tied to PCAOB review.
The Board's review of a small firm's exempt engagements, focused on audit quality and key personnel's independence and competence.

topics.topic_name: Conflicts of interest, studies and state regulators
topics.overview: Section 206 imposes a one-year cooling-off period before audit staff take a top finance role at the client. Section 207 ordered a study of mandatory firm rotation, Section 208 had the SEC write the independence rules, and Section 209 leaves standards for nonregistered firms to the states. SEC rules also bar contingent fees and audit partner pay for selling other services.
can_do: Apply the cooling-off rule to a hire from the audit firm
Tell what Title II required from what it only studied
Explain who sets standards for nonregistered accounting firms
Identify who acts as the audit committee when an issuer has none

subtopics.name: The Cooling-Off Period
subtopics.definition: Section 206 bars a firm from auditing an issuer whose top finance officer worked on its audit at the firm in the year before the audit began.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A former auditor in a top finance job may know and influence the audit approach. The one-year cooling-off period reduces that risk.
how_it_works: The covered roles are CEO, controller, CFO, chief accounting officer, or anyone in an equivalent position (Exchange Act Section 10A(l)).
The bar applies if the person was employed by the firm and took part in the audit in any capacity during the one-year period before the audit began.
SEC Rule 2-01(c)(2)(iii)(B) applies it to any financial reporting oversight role; audit procedures start the day after the prior annual report is filed.
The SEC rule excludes team members, other than the lead partner and quality reviewer, with 10 or fewer hours, and allows narrow merger and emergency exceptions.
The consequence falls on the firm: performing that audit is unlawful (Section 208(b)).
subtopics.example: Dev, a senior associate who worked on a pharmacy chain's audit, is offered the chain's director of financial reporting job, a financial reporting oversight role. Before accepting, Dev asks the firm's independence office, which compares Dev's last day on the engagement with the date the next audit's procedures will start.

review: Trace each finance executive's prior employer and audit team history
Compare the candidate's last audit work date with the one-year look-back window
evidence: Audit firm confirmation of the person's engagement hours and dates
Issuer's annual report filing date that starts the next audit
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee check prior audit-team service before the issuer fills any financial reporting oversight role.
audit_focus.decides: The audit committee oversees the hire's effect on auditor independence

subtopics.isaca_rule: A firm cannot audit an issuer whose CEO, CFO, controller, chief accounting officer or equivalent worked on that issuer's audit at the firm, in any capacity, during the year before the audit began.

exam_traps.trap: The cooling-off rule covers every former auditor in any job at the client.
exam_traps.why: Section 206 covers the CEO, controller, CFO, chief accounting officer and equivalents; the SEC rule extends it to financial reporting oversight roles, not every job.

exam_traps.trap: The rule applies only to former audit partners.
exam_traps.why: It covers anyone employed by the firm who took part in the audit in any capacity, subject to the SEC rule's 10-hour exclusion.

key_terms.definition: The one-year gap required between working on an issuer's audit and taking a top finance role there.
A role that can influence the financial statements, such as CEO, CFO, general counsel, controller or director of internal audit (Rule 2-01(f)(3)(ii)).

subtopics.name: SEC Rules and the Firm Rotation Study
subtopics.definition: Section 207 ordered a Comptroller General study of mandatory audit firm rotation, and Section 208 directed the SEC to write the rules carrying out Title II.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam items test what Title II required and what it only studied. Partners must rotate; audit firm rotation stayed a study topic.
how_it_works: The Comptroller General was to study the potential effects of mandatory firm rotation and report to Congress within one year (Section 207(a) and (b)).
Mandatory rotation means a limit on the years one firm may be the auditor of record for an issuer (Section 207(c)).
The SEC had to issue final rules carrying out Exchange Act Section 10A(g) to (l) within 180 days of enactment (Section 208(a)).
A firm may not issue an issuer's audit report while engaging in an activity those subsections or rules prohibit (Section 208(b)).
The SEC's independence rules are in Regulation S-X Rule 2-01 (17 CFR 210.2-01).
subtopics.example: Leah, a governance analyst at a pension fund, drafts a voting guideline saying U.S. law caps audit firm tenure. Before release, Leah checks Sections 203 and 207, rewrites it to say the law rotates partners while firm rotation was only studied, and keeps the fund's tenure limit as its own policy.

review: Compare internal statements on auditor tenure with Sections 203 and 207
Match every cited independence requirement against the current CFR text
evidence: GAO's published study on audit firm tenure, read for its findings
Current Rule 2-01 text from the electronic Code of Federal Regulations
audit_focus.recommend: Have the governance team present audit firm tenure limits as policy choices, not legal requirements.
