audit_focus.decides: The audit committee decides whether to keep or change the audit firm

subtopics.isaca_rule: Title II rotates partners, not firms: Section 207 only ordered a Comptroller General study of firm rotation. Section 208 had the SEC write the independence rules and made breaking them unlawful.

exam_traps.trap: The Act made audit firm rotation mandatory after a set number of years.
exam_traps.why: Section 207 asked the Comptroller General to study firm rotation; no section of the Act imposes it.

key_terms.definition: The head of the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the audit and investigations agency that works for Congress.
A limit on how many years one firm may be an issuer's auditor of record.

subtopics.name: State Regulators and Nonregistered Firms
subtopics.definition: Section 209 says state regulators should decide independently which standards apply to the nonregistered accounting firms they supervise, without presuming PCAOB standards apply.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most small accounting firms never audit issuers. Section 209 keeps PCAOB standards from spreading automatically to them through state licensing.
how_it_works: State regulatory authorities should make an independent determination of the proper standards for nonregistered firms (Section 209).
They consider the size and nature of the firms' business and of their clients' business.
PCAOB standards should not be presumed to apply to small and medium-sized nonregistered firms.
Registered firms stay under the Board, which reports inspection findings and sanctions to state regulators (Sections 104(g) and 105(d)).
subtopics.example: A state board of accountancy drafts rules for local firms that audit only private companies and charities. Ingrid, its staff counsel, advises the board to set standards suited to those firms' size and clients rather than copy the PCAOB's issuer standards, as Section 209 contemplates.

review: Read the state rulemaking record for analysis of local firm and client size
Confirm whether a firm is registered before applying Board standards
evidence: State board rule text and its stated basis
Board registration status of the firms covered
audit_focus.recommend: Have board staff record in the rulemaking file why each requirement suits the local firms it covers.
audit_focus.decides: Each state's licensing board decides; the PCAOB's reach stops at registered firms

subtopics.isaca_rule: State regulatory authorities should make an independent determination of the proper standards for the nonregistered firms they supervise, weighing firm and client size; PCAOB standards should not be presumed to apply to small and medium-sized nonregistered firms (Section 209).

exam_traps.trap: Section 209 requires states to apply PCAOB standards to every licensed firm.
exam_traps.why: Section 209 says the opposite: PCAOB standards should not be presumed to apply to small and medium-sized nonregistered firms.

key_terms.definition: An accounting firm not registered with the PCAOB, which therefore may not audit issuers.
The state body that licenses CPAs and accounting firms and supervises their practice.

subtopics.name: Who Counts as the Audit Committee
subtopics.definition: Section 205(a) defines the audit committee as the board committee that oversees accounting, financial reporting and audits or, if there is none, the entire board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Title II gives the audit committee real duties, such as preapproving auditor services and receiving the auditor's reports. The definition makes sure those duties land somewhere even at an issuer without a committee.
how_it_works: An audit committee is a committee or equivalent body set up by and among the board to oversee accounting, financial reporting and audits (Exchange Act Section 3(a)(58)(A)).
If an issuer has no such committee, the entire board of directors is its audit committee (Exchange Act Section 3(a)(58)(B)).
Section 205(b) also replaced 'independent public accountant' with 'registered public accounting firm' throughout Exchange Act Section 10A.
Duties such as preapproval (Section 202) and the auditor's reports (Section 204) then run to the whole board.
subtopics.example: Pinecrest Water, a utility that files Exchange Act reports after a registered bond offering, has no audit committee. When the auditor proposes a lease accounting review, Oluwaseun, the company secretary, puts the request on the full board's agenda before any work starts.

review: Confirm whether the issuer has a board committee overseeing financial reporting
Trace auditor service approvals to the body that acts as audit committee
evidence: Board and committee charters naming oversight duties
Minutes recording advance approval of each auditor engagement
audit_focus.recommend: Have the corporate secretary set a standing preapproval step for directors before the auditor starts any service.
audit_focus.decides: The entire board, acting as the audit committee, is responsible for preapproving the auditor's services

subtopics.isaca_rule: No audit committee does not mean no audit committee duties. Under Exchange Act Section 3(a)(58), added by Section 205(a), the entire board acts as the audit committee and owns preapproval and the auditor's reports.

exam_traps.trap: An issuer without an audit committee needs no preapproval of its auditor's services.
exam_traps.why: Section 205(a) treats the entire board as the audit committee, so Section 202 preapproval still applies.

key_terms.definition: The board committee overseeing accounting, financial reporting and audits or, if none exists, the entire board (15 U.S.C. 78c(a)(58)).
A change to another law that brings its wording into line with a new act, such as Section 205's edits to the Exchange Act.

subtopics.name: Partner Pay and Contingent Fees
subtopics.definition: SEC Rule 2-01 bars two money links between auditor and client: audit partner pay for selling other services, and contingent fees or commissions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Section 208 had the SEC write the independence rules. These two target mutual interest: an auditor who profits from outcomes or sales may lose objectivity.
how_it_works: An auditor that serves an audit client for a contingent fee or commission is not independent (17 CFR 210.2-01(c)(5), opened 31 Oct 2026).
A contingent fee depends on a specified finding or result; fees may still vary with complexity, and court-fixed fees are not contingent (210.2-01(f)(10)).
Independence is also lost if an audit partner is paid for selling the client services other than audit, review or attest work (210.2-01(c)(8), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Firms with fewer than ten partners and fewer than five issuer audit clients are exempt from the compensation rule (210.2-01(c)(8), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Approving the service does not cure either breach; both rules turn on how the money is earned.
subtopics.example: Grace, the head of independence at a large firm, reviews the audit partners' bonus plan before the new year. Grace removes a bonus tied to cross-selling consulting work to audit clients and rewrites a fee letter for an audit client's systems project so the fee no longer depends on savings achieved.

review: Compare audit partner bonus criteria with the Rule 2-01(c)(8) bar
Inspect fee terms in each non-audit engagement letter for result-based pricing
evidence: Partner compensation plan and bonus calculation records
Signed engagement letters showing how each fee is set
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee obtain the firm's yearly written confirmation on partner pay and fee terms.
audit_focus.decides: The firm sets pay and fees; the audit committee oversees independence

subtopics.isaca_rule: An auditor loses independence if it works for an audit client on a contingent fee or commission, or if an audit partner is paid for selling the client non-audit services, outside the small-firm exemption.

exam_traps.trap: A fee that varies with the work's complexity is a contingent fee.
exam_traps.why: Rule 2-01(f)(10) says fees may vary with complexity; a fee is contingent when it depends on a finding or result.

exam_traps.trap: Audit committee preapproval makes a partner's sales bonus acceptable.
exam_traps.why: Rule 2-01(c)(8) concerns the partner's pay, not the service; approving the service does not change the impairment.

key_terms.definition: A fee charged only if, or in an amount set by, a specified finding or result.
A payment tied to selling or referring a product or service.

key_terminologies.PCAOB: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board: a nonprofit corporation, under SEC oversight, that oversees the audit firms of issuers.
key_terminologies.SEC: The Securities and Exchange Commission: oversees issuers and the PCAOB, approves Board rules and reviews Board sanctions.
key_terminologies.Issuer: A company with SEC-registered securities, or required to file Exchange Act reports, or with a pending registration statement.
key_terminologies.Registered public accounting firm: An audit firm registered with the PCAOB; only these may audit issuers.
key_terminologies.Associated person: A partner, accountant, employee or contractor who shares in a registered firm's profits or acts for it on audit reports.
key_terminologies.Accounting support fee: The annual fee, allocated mainly among issuers by market capitalization, that funds the PCAOB and FASB.
key_terminologies.Inspection: The PCAOB's review of a registered firm's audits and quality control: yearly above 100 issuer clients, otherwise at least every three years.
key_terminologies.Concurring partner review: Second-partner review and approval of each audit report, required by Section 103.
key_terminologies.Audit workpapers: The records supporting an audit report, kept at least seven years under Section 103 and Rule 2-06.
key_terminologies.FASB: The Financial Accounting Standards Board, the private standard setter the SEC recognizes under Section 108.
key_terminologies.Foreign public accounting firm: A firm organized under foreign law; if it audits issuers it is subject to the Act like a U.S. firm.
key_terminologies.Non-audit service: Any professional service to an issuer other than the audit or review of its financial statements.
key_terminologies.Prohibited services: The nine non-audit services an issuer's auditor may not provide during the audit, listed in Section 201.
key_terminologies.Preapproval: The audit committee's advance approval of every audit and permitted non-audit service by its auditor.
key_terminologies.De minimis exception: A narrow waiver of preapproval for small, unrecognized non-audit services approved before the audit ends.
key_terminologies.Partner rotation: The rule that lead and reviewing partners leave an issuer's audit after five consecutive years.
key_terminologies.Mandatory firm rotation: A limit on how long one firm may audit an issuer; studied under Section 207, not required.
key_terminologies.Cooling-off period: The one-year bar on auditing an issuer whose top finance officer worked on its audit at the firm.
key_terminologies.Comptroller General: The head of the Government Accountability Office, which Section 207 directed to study firm rotation.
key_terminologies.Emerging growth company (EGC): A newly public issuer under a revenue cap; some PCAOB rules do not apply to its audits.
key_terminologies.Section 10A: The Exchange Act section where Title II placed the auditor independence rules (subsections g to l).
key_terminologies.Audit partner: A partner covered by SEC rotation rules: the lead partner, the quality reviewer and other decision-making partners, not technical consultants.
key_terminologies.Contingent fee: A fee that depends on a finding or result; providing any service to an audit client on one impairs independence.
